In researching what components I wanted to put on my touring bike, I came across a lot of forum posts and articles all repeating the same thing: for stopping power, the best rim brake is a V-brake. Cantilevers are weaker in comparison. If you have them, swap them out for V-brakes. Cantilevers are also harder to adjust than V-brakes.

Seeing this repeated so often, I began to accept it. But is it really true? The first time I really started doubting it was when I read the following page: http://www.sheldonbrown.com/cantilever-geometry.html

I'll spare you from having to read the whole page. The "aha" moment came from reading this part:

The new direct-pull cantilevers, such as Shimano's "V" brakes, also have a fixed mechanical advantage. Since their pivots are below the level of the rim, smaller wheels give more mechanical advantage, rather than less as with caliper brakes. Traditional cantilever brakes, however, allow the mechanic to adjust the mechanical advantage to a considerable extent, mainly by adjusting the length of the transverse cable and the height of the cable yoke.

We just learned 2 important things here. Number one is that linear/direct pull V-brakes are actually a newer type of Cantilever brakes. In fact, if you go on reading that page, you'll eventually discover that by doing some magic with the cable, traditional cantilevers can be used as linear pull V-brakes! The number two thing we learned here is that V-brakes are less adjustable than the traditional Cantilevers.

That second bit is probably the most important. If I'm correct, then presumably, medium profile or low profile Cantilevers with the right transverse and yoke adjustments may be able to function comparably to a V-brake.

But if this is seeming confusing to you, I don't blame you. If you read the whole page, you'd have a better idea of what's being discussed. The versatility of Cantilever adjustment is probably one of the reasons people say they're too complicated. In reality, I don't think they are. Having seen several youtube videos instructing the viewer how to set them up, they look really, really simple to me, and easy to service. They also make getting the brake pads out of the way when replacing a flat tube much easier.

I also came across this: http://www.rodbikes.com/articles/brakes.html

So what do you think? Is everybody wrong? With a little knowledge, are the traditional Cantilevers actually preferable to V-brakes?
Is the conventional wisdom about Cantilever vs V-brakes wrong?
